# Your way is short; my poison is fatal

### *[October of Zarathustra](https://bradydale.com/series-october-of-zarathustra.html)*

A long time ago now, I was an organizer. I worked in churches in Tallahassee, Florida. I was the first organizer for a local organization called the Tallahassee Equality Action Ministry, or TEAM. It was an affiliate of this thing called [the DART Center](https://thedartcenter.org/), out of Florida. 

This was a network working to keep the [Saul Alinsky](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Saul_Alinsky) model of organizing alive. If that means anything to you (It's not really worth going into, to be honest). The point is just that I was knocking on doors of churches, working to get them into a coalition that would pour its people into various social change efforts.

The job wasn't recruiting people one-by-one. It was getting in front of people who already led people, and recruiting them.

> On *Thus Spoke Zarathustra*, part 1, chapters 18 to 21: "Little Old and Young Women," "The Adder's Bite," "Children and Marriage" and "Voluntary Death."

There were a handful of really big churches in town. They were the mama jamas that everyone knew were *the ones* to get in the fold to really crank the power up. This was 20 years ago. One of the pastors of one of the churches, while very successful, was known as being a hard guy to reach.

But I called him one day and he said, sure, he'd take a meeting with me. This seemed like a real coup.

Then I got to the church at the appointed time, he walked in with a young woman, introduced her to me, and walked away. I had been pawned off on an associate pastor. In other words: nothing was going to happen. We were going to have a pointless chat that would waste time for both us.

Now looking back on it, I'm not disappointed that my stint with this group didn't work out (it didn't). If anything, I wish I had gotten out of organizing sooner, but I did learn some lessons from it. One principle the DART crew taught was that organizers honor their commitments and, in doing so, hold other people accountable for honoring theirs.

[![](https://bradydale.com/blyg/media/af54afa712d0a69ac62bd7f09e21f9bc7f122804f76894346c51dc0939703483.png)](https://www.uutallahassee.org/wp-content/uploads/2015/07/MPP_June_17_2015_reformatted.pdf?utm_source=chatgpt.com)

What I should have done when I was pawned off on the lackey was said, "Listen, you said you were going to meet with me. That was your commitment. If you're not honoring it, then I'm not going to honor mine, either."

And left.

I doubt it would have changed the outcome, but it would have earned a little respect. He was making a power move. And the right answer for a power move is another power move.

Now — the very best move is *no power moves*. It's just being normal. Don't take the meeting if you don't want the meeting!

But if someone does pull a power move on you, pull one back. You've nothing to lose. I didn't that day, and it's bugged me ever since.

That's what I got out of the chapter, "On the Adder's Bite," in particular. That's all about taking the sting out of the harm people try to do you. But it's also the greater theme across these chapters. Nietzsche doesn't seem to be making a general guide to life here.

*Thus Spoke Zarathustra* seems more like Diogenes' lantern. It's a book searching for one reader.

## One line

> “He who bears injustice alone is hideous to behold.” —Zarathustra

—Brady Dale  
October 6, 2026

**Next Zarathustra:** [The highest virtue is uncommon and useless](https://bradydale.com/80.html)
